scenario: WIBTA if I forced my son to play sports or some other extracurricular? | I’ve been seriously contemplating forcing my 13 year old to play sports. Not because I want to force my dreams on him or something of the sort, but because he is incredibly LAZY to the point it internally frustrates me. He gets straight C’s in MIDDLE SCHOOL, gets in trouble for talking in class all the time, doesn’t clean up after himself ever (will literally eat his food and just leave it sitting there either downstairs or in his room for DAYS!!) , and generally speaking does absolutely nothing but sit around the house playing games. He doesn’t even shower unless told (will walk around the house with the same clothes on for a week during breaks). He’s one of those people that would rather be comfortable doing nothing and being stagnant in life, than leaving his comfort zone and being productive. Basically he doesn’t do anything he doesn’t want to do unless he absolutely has to. His mother, who I have shared visitation with, is in my opinion an absolutely terrible parent. She doesn’t push him to do anything. She just enables this sort of behavior by cleaning up after his messes, and barely punishing him for anything. I fear he’s shaping up to be a loser. I’ve been thinking of taking the initiative by forcing him to be apart of some team oriented extracurricular activity in order to snap these terrible bad habits, and complete lack of a work ethic. Something tells me being around friends of similar age all working really hard towards something and having fun in the process would give him the jolt he needs. My current thinking is telling him he has to play basketball for 1 season and if he doesn’t like it he can quit after the season is over. Would that make me an asshole? TL;DR: 13 year old son is lazy, so WIBTA if I forced him to play sports for a season to activate some sort of work ethic?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for a parent to force their 13-year-old son to play sports or join some extracurricular activity. The parent is really frustrated because the son is super lazy, gets bad grades, doesn't clean up after himself, and just sits around playing games all day. The mom isn't helping either; she's enabling the behavior by cleaning up his messes and not setting any boundaries. The dad wants to force his son into basketball for a season to try and instill some work ethic and get him out of his comfort zone. First, I need to understand the parent's perspective. They're worried that their son is heading down a bad path and that without intervention, he might end up being unproductive and unsuccessful in life. They see sports or extracurricular activities as a way to teach him responsibility, teamwork, and discipline. It's a common belief that participating in sports can help build character and work ethic in kids. On the other hand, forcing a child into an activity they don't want to do could have negative consequences. It might lead to resentment between the parent and child, and the child might resist even more. There's also the risk that the child could develop a negative association with sports or extracurricular activities, making them less likely to engage in them voluntarily in the future. I wonder if there are other ways to encourage the child without forcing him. Maybe setting up a reward system for completing chores or doing well in school could motivate him. Or perhaps finding an activity that he's actually interested in, which would make him more willing to participate. It's also important to consider the child's feelings and opinions. At 13, he's old enough to have some say in what he wants to do. Maybe the parent could have a conversation with him about why it's important to be active and responsible, and try to find a compromise. Another thing to think about is the role of the other parent. If the mom isn't supporting the dad's efforts, it might make it harder to enforce any changes. The parents need to be on the same page to effectively address the child's behavior. I also think about the long-term effects of forcing someone into an activity. While it might provide short-term benefits like improved grades or better behavior, it might not lead to lasting changes if the child doesn't feel motivated or interested in what they're doing. Maybe the parent could start small, encouraging the child to try something new without making it feel like a punishment. Building up from there could help the child gradually become more active and responsible. In conclusion, while the parent's intentions are good, forcing the child into sports or extracurricular activities might not be the best approach. It's important to consider the child's feelings, find activities that interest him, and work together as a family to encourage positive behavior and responsibility.
